lesson.title: Farben I: rot, blau, grün, schwarz, bunt
lesson.subtitle: the first row of colors — three twins, one half-lost twin, and the honest odd one out

hook.title: Three Twins, a Ghost, and a Mystery
hook.content: Color words are ancient — most of this row is older than the countries that speak it — and the five show every kind of kinship at once. rot ↔ red is the badge one: the same Proto-Germanic word, *raudaz, with English keeping the D and German hardening it to T — the d_to_t family, the same law that made day into Tag. blau ↔ blue and grün ↔ green are pure twins, no shift at all: German and English read the same sky and the same forest. schwarz ↔ swart is the ghost: the same word on both sides, but everyday English retired it — it survives only in the poetic swarthy — while German still says schwarz for everything dark. And then bunt: no twin, no borrowing anyone can prove, its origin still argued over by German etymologists. Every family has one member like this, and the honest answer is the lesson: bunt means colorful, and its past is a blur. One bonus twin rides along — weiß ↔ white, the mountain's December color.

footnotes.title: The Flag Reads Itself
footnotes.content: Die deutsche Fahne ist schwarz, rot und gold — the German flag is black, red and gold. Two of the flag's three colors are in this lesson, and das Gold has been yours since lesson 101. The sentence needs only one new word, die Fahne (the flag) — the colors do the rest, which is exactly what a first-row color lesson is for.

pattern.title: Colors Stand After sein
pattern.content: Four frames, one rule. 1. With sein, the color never changes: Die Blume ist rot, der Himmel ist blau, der Wald ist grün, die Katze ist schwarz, der Vogel ist bunt — no ending, no gender agreement, the adjective just stands. 2. Two colors stack with und: Die Katze ist schwarz und weiß. 3. The month frame fronts and swaps: Im Dezember ist der Berg weiß — the time phrase takes position 1 and pushes ist to slot 2, the swap you know from Heute lerne ich Deutsch. 4. The count: Null Blumen im Dezember — null is your lesson-5122 zero, counting what the snow replaced.
pattern.linguist_note: English black and German schwarz are not twins: black is the Germanic 'burned' word — kin to bleach, the burned one and the bright one from one root — while English's real black-twin swart was pushed into poetry. German kept schwarz as the everyday word and never needed a replacement. Color words are the slowest-moving layer of a language, which is why this row is a museum of every kinship type.

exercises.prompt: The first row of colors — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: Zero flowers in December — the mountain is white
matching_pairs.german: Null Blumen im Dezember — der Berg ist weiß

matching_pairs.english: The rug is green, the wardrobe is black
matching_pairs.german: Der Teppich ist grün, der Schrank ist schwarz

matching_pairs.english: The curtain is blue, the flowers on the balcony are colorful
matching_pairs.german: Der Vorhang ist blau, die Blumen auf dem Balkon sind bunt

exercises.target_answer: Die Blume ist rot, Der Himmel ist blau, Der Wald ist grün, Die Katze ist schwarz, Der Vogel ist bunt, Null Blumen im Dezember — der Berg ist weiß, Der Schal ist bunt, Der Teppich ist grün, der Schrank ist schwarz, Der Vorhang ist blau, die Blumen auf dem Balkon sind bunt
exercises.meaning: red flower, blue sky, green forest, black cat, colorful bird, white mountain in December
exercises.explanation: The color stands after sein and never takes an ending: rot, blau, grün, schwarz, bunt. And the December count is null — zero flowers — because the mountain took over in weiß, the twin of white.

exercises.prompt: Which color wears the D→T badge — German T where English keeps D (Tag ↔ day)?
exercises.explanation: rot and red are the same Proto-Germanic word: English kept the D, German hardened it to T — the same road Tag took from day. blau, grün and schwarz are twins without a shift, and bunt stays out of the quiz: no twin, no proven loan.

exercises.prompt: 'schwarz' has an English twin that everyday English retired — it survives only in a poetic word. Which one?
exercises.meaning: schwarz ↔ swart/swarthy: the same word, English kept only the ghost
exercises.explanation: Both come from Proto-Germanic *swartz, Old English sweart. German still says schwarz every day; English kept the word only as the poetic swarthy — a twin living in the attic.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'In December the mountain is white'
exercises.target_answer: Im Dezember ist der Berg weiß
exercises.meaning: In December the mountain is white
exercises.explanation: The month phrase takes position 1 and pushes ist to slot 2 — the same swap as Jetzt lerne ich Deutsch. And weiß wears the T→S badge: English kept the T in white, German turned it to ss, exactly like Wasser from water.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The sky is blue and the forest is green'
exercises.target_answer: Der Himmel ist blau und der Wald ist grün
exercises.meaning: The sky is blue and the forest is green
exercises.explanation: Two sein-frames joined by und, the verb second in each half. Swap the nouns and the colors still fit: der Himmel ist blau, der Wald ist grün, die Blume ist rot, der Vogel ist bunt.

summary.outcome: Say five colors after sein without inflecting them, spot the D→T badge on rot, and keep weiß and bunt in the December picture.

use_example.german: Im Dezember ist der Berg weiß — null Blumen, aber der Himmel ist blau.
use_example.english: In December the mountain is white — zero flowers, but the sky is blue.

summary.takeaway: rot wears D→T (red kept the D), blau and grün are pure twins, schwarz survives in English only as swarthy, bunt's origin is honestly unknown — and weiß is white with the T→S badge.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: braun, grau, rosa, lila — and die Farbe, the head noun that colors them all.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Farben I: rot, blau, grün, schwarz, bunt (The sky is blue and the forest is green):
twist.target_answer: Der Himmel ist blau und der Wald ist grün
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Himmel ist blau und der Wald ist grün" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Farben I: rot, blau, grün, schwarz, bunt without relying on short-term echo.

rot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *raudaz; English red is the same root — English d ↔ German t. [wiktionary]

blau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *blēwaz; English blue (via French bleu) is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

grün.context_phrase: Im Sommer ist das Gras grün.
grün.context_translation: In summer the grass is green.
grün.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *grōniz, the root of grow; English green is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

schwarz.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *swartaz — the true English twin is swart/swarthy; English black is a different Germanic word. [wiktionary]

bunt.etymology_derivation: Probably from Latin punctus, a relative of English point — no English color-word cognate; memorize this one. [wiktionary]

schal.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English shawl, from Persian šâl — a loan, not an inherited cognate. [wiktionary]

teppich.context_phrase: Der Teppich liegt unter dem Tisch.
teppich.context_translation: The rug is under the table.
teppich.etymology_derivation: Via Medieval Latin tapicus, from Latin tapes; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

schrank.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skrankaz 'grid, barrier'; no English cognate — memorize this one (see der Kühlschrank). [wiktionary]

vorhang.etymology_derivation: vor (in front) + hängen (hang) — 'the front-hang'; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

balkon.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French balcon, Italian balcone — a Romance loan; no Germanic root. [wiktionary]

null.etymology_derivation: From Italian nulla, Latin nullus 'none' — the same Latin loan as English null. [wiktionary]

dezember.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin december, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

berg.context_phrase: Der Berg ist im Winter weiß.
berg.context_translation: The mountain is white in winter.
berg.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bërg, from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. English barrow, a burial hill, is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

weiß.etymology_derivation: t → ß. Also first-person of wissen (ich weiß = I know/am wise).

blume.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *blōmō 'blossom'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

himmel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *himil — the same Germanic line as English heaven's root family. [wiktionary]

wald.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *walþu — cognate with Old English weald, surviving in weald/wold. [wiktionary]

katze.context_phrase: Die Katze schläft auf dem Sofa.
katze.context_translation: The cat sleeps on the sofa.

vogel.context_translation: The bird sings in the garden.
vogel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fuglaz, likely from 'to fly' — cognate with English fowl. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
